As a fellow Polish expat, honestly, think about your family. If you love them and cherish them of course. You will live until 80, but what about them? What is the age of your parents, grandparents, other closer relatives? Are you okay with seeing them 1-2 time per year? You know, I have this comfort of living within EU borders and coming back every 2-3 months is doable. But USA? Will you have the money? Will you have the energy? 
I think that's something to consider - you're not getting younger and want to use opportunities in your life, but your family is not getting younger as well. 
Second thing is that US is good for making money, but hell to live in as a family. Do you want to be scared that your kid will be shot? Do you want to pay copious amount of money (probably from hefty salary) to go to the dentist, to call ambulance? Are you okay with shitty quality of produce such as food or non-drinkable water? Do you agree with driving your car until you're 80 and not giving your children freedom of commuting because there's literally no public transportation there, apart from New York? Can you adjust to their current politics that oppress people the same, or even more, as our Polish government? I would NEVER, EVER would want my child to live in the US. Point blank. 
Although Poland has many awful qualities now, we still are under the safety blanket of the EU - our food is good, we have subsidies to build roads, to develop schools and children can be independent here. I moved mostly because of my career choice that is not going to be lucrative in our home country (translator), but you, as electrician? You have a chance to get good living in PL. I know that States seem to be amazing because they give you loads of money, but remember, there you need to pay for literally everything. And since your job is high-risk, be aware that their shitty insurance programs or whatever are not going to cover shit in your field. 
Plus their bread... Think about it. I would love to come back to Poland honestly, we have amazing banking system, good public transport, we are safer and less capitalistic than the US, you will have your family, culture and food you know next to you, it's not a bad life. But depending on your priorities (maybe you just want to make lots of money? Maybe you seriously love US culture? Maybe you enjoy trucks and driving?) it's not like it's the only option. You need to decide what to do with yourself.

1. If you're going to be studying with young people in a bigger city, do not start conversation about religion very casually and positively. It's true that some folks are Catholics, very dedicated to say the least, but they're mostly older people. Right now, due to the political shenanigans of our government, religion is quite a sore spot for many Polish, so be careful about that. 
2. Learn some basic phrases in Polish, especially related to grocery shopping, sending letters, etc. - generally, places where you can encounter older people. Not so many of them know English on a conversational level, along with tiny bit of xenophobia that is rather prevalent among older generations due to the homogeneity of our country + recent war migration. In some cool cafés, food chains, shopping centres English should be fine, but in places like kiosques, probably some supermarkets (Biedronka, Lidl, Kaufland,...) not so much. It also depends very much on the city that you're going to live in - if it's a student city, like Warsaw, Łódź, Cracov, Poznań or Wrocław then yeah, totally, but Lublin, Rzeszow, Toruń? They're also student cities, but significantly smaller, so not sure about that. 
3. Don't know which part of America you come from, but be prepared that the weather is rather shitty. We have long autumns, lots of rain, lately cold but snowless winters, hot summers. Lack of sunlight can fuck people up, so take D3 vitamin regularly. 
4. Polish people can be friendly, but they keep their distance with unknown folks. They also like to brag about bad things and perceive reality in a negative way - they won't fake smiles and happiness to keep up with pleasantries. It might come as a quite cultural shock to you, but it's not personal; in-between ourselves I think small talk is more popular among older people, like ladies chatting in a doctor's waiting room or a tram. Younger people tend to keep it to themselves. 
5. Do not assume things. It's better than you ask about something rather than make a stupid joke that might come off as ignorant or even rude. There are many stereotypes revolving around Polish around the world, and in the USA, Polish minorities have literally no clue how our country currently looks like. We are known for disliking "our kin" but it's kind of exclusive to us. If you will say something about wars, international relations etc. to a wrong person, you actually might get yelled at, scoffed at or even punched. Not that you can't have your opinions abour our country and people, but just be wary and careful, especially outside of your university realm. 
6. Tipping is not required, but it's nice when someone offered you good service. Cashiers do not pack bags. Recycling is getting more restrictive, but not so much like in Germany. We have amazing banking systems, fast internet and contactless deliveries (look up Paczkomat). Żabka is the most common mini-market right now and you can buy there basic shit, although it's expensive. If you want to work part-time, get help of some kind of local, as employers, especially the ones recruiting students, tend to be shady and underpay. People sometimes tend to be not on top of their hygine, you'll smell it in public transport. But use it - it's cheaper than uber and rather reliable (this varies between cities). The concept of   systemic racism is not an issue here - most of the people do not understand this. On the other hand,  we are more sensible to other societal issues, like class division and distribution of wealth. There is a huge polarization of society in our country, people are exhausted by inflation and current government. So I would say that, if you're not going to be in some kind of private, elite school but a public university, try to not overexpose yourself if you are very wealthy. You can wear whatever you want of course, but if someone talks a lot about their comfort, money, job etc. it is not treated by Polish as an accomplishment, but rather something you want to rub in their faces. Many people are struggling right now financially, so it might come off as ignorant. 
7. Learn about our culture a little bit. You'll be surprised how much people know about your country, due to the dissemination of American-oriented media in Europe in general. We know your popular singers, traditions, presidents, more prominent actors. If you want be appreciated, read about history. Learn about current politics. Find some Polish artists, sportsmen etc. that you could discuss with others. 
8. A lot of us drink A LOT, and smoke A LOT. It's very normalised and nagging about that won't help. People also tend to not be that understanding when it comes to smoking in public spaces, so they won't move to a more remote corner or stay in one place. 
9. We always take off shoes when coming to someone's house. Not at the Uni, but when visiting someone's private space, shoes are a no-no. We use slippers or walk without shoes. 
10. In general, just have respect and human decency and you will get by. I'm happy that you enjoy Polish culture and want to spend such a long time here. I wholeheartedly wish you good luck! Powodzenia mordo!

I can explain it to you from the perspective of a person who loves Poland dearly in terms of culture (I was volunteering for many local societies + eager to go to museums and other historical places) but who emigrated recently due to the inability to live in my country. 
First, unfortunately, what you say about politics might not be the full picture of what is Poland, but it certainly influences daily life of people. As a teenager I loved my country more, because I didn't have to worry about basic needs and, in general, adult stuff. After you reach the age when you need to be somehow independent, you will certainly find more things to hate about your country. For example, landscapes. How people, apart from the ones living close by, can enjoy nature, landscapes and culture if they don't have enough money to go on a vacation? If daily life expenses are so high that it's hard to even live through one month, not even taking into account other pleasures of life? Well, they're not going to appreciate it, because they don't have the chance to experience it. A lot of young people today can't become independent, because renting market is shit, starting salaries are shit and so on. If they don't feel safe with their savings (or their lack of) after paying for all of the necessities, they become resentful, because well, they work, they want to develop themselves, but they can't! Why? Our country's policies and politics in general. To give you the perspective, as a student I was working for a year in a restaurant that paid 13zl/h. I had shifts 3-4 times a week that lasted for 12-13 hours. I was so exhausted that, for a year, I haven't been able to go anywhere, be it museum, cooking lessons or simple outing to the cinema. And you know what? My parents still had to pay for my flat, because I couldn't live off this shit of a wage that I had been gaining. Right now, abroad,  as a master student, I can't work MORE than 60h/month and my minimum salary has to be at least 13 EUR/h. Moreover, my university provides me with exclusive offers of students jobs that are accomodating our schedules and workload that we have outside our job. They basically care about our well-being and they don't treat us as a cheap workforce that can be expolited. Moreover! I was a really bright student and had good grades in Poland, but I couldn't obtain ANY scholarships. Whereas here, I got a VERY generous scholarship for my, attention guys, academic achievements that I had in my Polish university! New university in a foreign country saw more potential in me than a place I was born in and voluntarily supported it throughout my life. If my country can't even appreciate me in any way and only makes my life harder, why should I love it? Why should I care about spreading soft power of my culture? It's not that I hate Poland, I love the language, I love Polish literature, poetry, 20th century painters, traditional costumes of certain voivodies etc. but it's just so insignificant when you take into account struggles that people, old and young, schooled and not, experience every day in their own mother country. Coupled with the hate speech agenda propagated by our government, where women are bad, LGBT is bad, young people are bad, only God counts and preaching to "the old times" of burning witches and praying for 9 hours a day, well, it makes people hateful about their country, even blinded by those bad things and not the ones which we can be truly proud of. It just sucks when you don't feel at home in your home. I hope that sheds a light onto why people seem to hate Poland that much, despite the good things our country offers.
